title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction is the most common cause of pediatric hydronephrosis and a frequent condition encountered by pediatric urologists, nephrologists, and primary care providers. Early recognition and appropriate management are essential to preserve renal function, prevent recurrent urinary tract infections, and optimize long-term outcomes. This continuing medical education activity provides an in-depth review of the etiology, pathophysiology, and diagnostic evaluation of UPJ obstruction in the pediatric population. Learners can expect to be presented with current evidence-based strategies for imaging modalities, including ultrasound, diuretic renography, and MRI urography, along with clinical indicators for intervention. Both surgical and non-surgical treatment options will be discussed, with an emphasis on minimally invasive pyeloplasty techniques and long-term follow-up considerations. By participating in this activity, the interprofessional team—including physicians, advanced practice providers, nurses, and allied health professionals—will gain improved competence in recognizing early signs, coordinating diagnostic workups, and implementing effective treatment plans tailored to each child’s needs. This course empowers healthcare professionals with the knowledge and tools necessary to enhance collaborative care, strengthen patient-family communication, and improve outcomes for children affected by UPJ obstruction.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Introduction
content: The kidneys have a crucial role in regulating fluid and electrolyte balance, as well as blood pressure and hemoglobin levels. During fetal life, the kidneys develop from the metanephric mesoderm up to the distal tubules. The collecting duct, major and minor calyces, renal pelvis, and ureters arise from the ureteric bud, which originates from the mesonephric duct during the fifth week of the intrauterine phase. This explains that the ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) is wholly made by the ureteric bud rather than the fusion of two different mesenchymal tissues.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Introduction
content: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) is a well-recognized clinical entity that impairs urine flow from the renal pelvis into the ureter and, if undetected and untreated, can lead to complete loss of the affected kidney. UPJO is most commonly a congenital condition that can be detected by routine antenatal ultrasound during the second trimester, but is also commonly identified incidentally during workup for recurrent UTIs in childhood and adolescence. [1] [2] It can also be caused by entities such as retroperitoneal processes or post-surgical ureteral scarring. Causes of this vary between children and adults. [3]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology
content: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) is either a congenital or acquired disease, with the former being the most common etiology. [4]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology -- Congenital Causes
content: Ureteral hypoplasia may lead to a narrowed aperistaltic segment of the ureter in which the circular muscle fibers are replaced by abnormal longitudinal muscle with fibrous tissue, which in turn will impair the urine drainage from the renal pelvis into the ureter and cause functional obstruction.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology -- Congenital Causes
content: Entrapment of the ureter by a crossing accessory renal vessel, most commonly from the lower pole. This results in the kinking of the proximal ureter, interrupting the free flow of the urine. This contributes to almost 50% of the surgically treated UPJO in symptomatic children and adolescents. [5]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology -- Congenital Causes
content: High insertion of the ureter into the renal pelvis can result in the failure of urine emptying from the pelvis into the ureter. This can be either primary or secondary to ureteral hypoplasia or renal scarring. Normally, the ureter is inserted into the most dependent part of the renal pelvis, allowing free urine flow, while a highly inserted ureter will cause acute angulation in the ureteropelvic junction, leading to functional obstruction with hydronephrosis.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology -- Extrinsic
content: This is mainly caused by an external compression on the ureteropelvic junction or the proximal ureter. Retroperitoneal fibrosis Retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy (eg, testicular cancer, lymphoma) Retroperitoneal mass (eg, sarcoma) Retroperitoneal freely mobile kidney might cause positional obstruction, by which the pressure on the ureter is affected by the position of the patient. [3] [4]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Etiology -- Intrinsic
content: Ureteral wall and peri-ureteral scarring can result from an impacted stone, chronic inflammation, or radiation. Ureteric tumors, such as malignant urothelial cell carcinoma, or benign lesions like fibroepithelial polyps. Iatrogenic Post-endoscopic procedures, such as ureteroscopy or endopyelotomy After open surgical procedures such as pyelolithotomy or failed repair of a primary UPJO [6]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Epidemiology
content: Ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) is more commonly seen in the pediatric age group rather than adults, and this anatomical pathology is seen more frequently in boys than in girls, with up to twice the number of cases in males compared to females. The left side is affected twice as often as the right side. Bilateral UPJO occurs in 10% to 40% of cases.  It is the most common cause of antenatally detected hydronephrosis, accounting for approximately 80% of cases. [7] The incidence of this is about 1 in 1000 to 1500 live births., and the incidence in adults is not well characterized. [3] [8]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Pathophysiology
content: Several proposed factors contribute to UPJO: Abnormal pressure within the renal pelvis and its compliance, which is affected by the urine volume produced, the internal diameter of the UPJ, and the collecting system. Decreased peristaltic activity of the ureter, due to collagen deposits within the smooth muscle arrangements and decreased/thin smooth muscle fibers with decreased neural components. This is supported histologically in both murine and human samples from pyeloplasty (see histology section below). [4]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Pathophysiology
content: A less common congenital cause of ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) is an accessory renal vessel arising from the renal vessels, aorta, vena cava, or iliac vessels, which can interfere with the collecting system. Stenosis of the UPJ can also be acquired from the previously mentioned causes, leading to reactive fibrosis in the affected ureteral segment, and annular strictures may develop.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Pathophysiology
content: Most of the UPJOs are partial. In this type of obstruction, the urothelium increases production of vasoactive peptides and cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-5 and eotaxin-2, which act as chemoattractants for leukocytes, leading to inflammatory cell infiltration. By altering eicosanoid production in the kidney, monocytic infiltration is believed to affect renal blood flow and decrease the total GFR in the affected kidney. However, single-nephron GFR will be increased. Similarly, activation of the renin-angiotensin system can reduce the GFR of the affected kidney through its vasoconstrictor effect. Murine models also implicate the sonic hedghog and TGF-ß pathways. [4] [7] [8]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Histopathology
content: Grossly, smooth muscle hypertrophy, perifasicular fibrosis, and inflammatory cell infiltration, with a notably intact epithelial layer, can be seen. Microscopically, increased collagen deposition can be seen in the smooth muscle layer with thin muscle fibers and decreased neural components. [4]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- History and Physical
content: The condition is usually detected during antenatal ultrasonography at 20 weeks of gestation and is not associated with any antenatal complications.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- History and Physical
content: Pediatric ureteropelvic junction obstruction might be associated with other congenital anomalies such as an imperforated anus, multicystic kidney, and ipsilateral ureterovesical reflux; in such patients, ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) should be treated first. Up to 50% of infants with UPJO have some other urologic abnormality. In cases of a duplex renal system, the lower moiety is more commonly affected, and ureterovesical reflux is often found and can be diagnosed with a voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG). Common symptoms in older children: Intermittent abdominal or flank pain, often worse with increased fluid intake Recurrent UTIs or pyelonephritis Vomiting Fever Hematuria secondary to infection Uncommonly, an abdominal mass may be palpated [9]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- History and Physical
content: Adults present with symptoms similar to those in the pediatric age group; especially intermittent flank pain. Usually, it is associated with increased fluid intake and diuretics, such as tea and coffee. [6] [7] On examination, patients may present with other signs of urinary tract infections or pyelonephritis, like fevers, chills. rigors, or hematuria.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Evaluation -- Laboratory Findings
content: All patients who have symptoms of ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) should have a full set of labs including complete blood count, renal function tests, including creatinine and BUN. Patients will present with elevated creatinine and decreased GFR.  In cases of infection, leukocytosis can be seen. A urine sample should be sent for analysis and culture as urinary tract infections are commonly seen in these patients.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Evaluation -- Imaging
content: Ultrasonography Hydronephrosis can be detected as an incidental finding on antenatal ultrasound, which might reflect underlying UPJO. In neonates who were found to have mild to moderate hydronephrosis on an antenatal scan, a follow-up scan should be done after 48 hours, to avoid transient neonatal dehydration period. However, in severe cases, a scan should be performed within the first 48 hours in case urgent intervention is needed. [10] The Society for Fetal Urology (SFU) grading system is used to evaluate the severity of hydronephrosis as follows: Grade 0 - No hydronephrosis, intact central renal complex seen on ultrasound Grade 1 - Only renal pelvis visualized, dilated pelvis on ultrasound, no caliectasis Grade 2 - Moderately dilated renal pelvis and a few calyces Grade 3 - Hydronephrosis with nearly all calyces seen, large renal pelvis without parenchymal thinning Grade 4 - Severe dilatation of renal pelvis and calyces with accompanying parenchymal atrophy or thinning

content: It should be kept in mind that almost 20% of antenatally detected hydronephrosis resolves after birth.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Evaluation
content: Functional Renography Most commonly, the technetium-99m Mercaptoacetyltriglycine (99mTc-MAG-3) nuclear renal scan  is used to determine the split function of each kidney and to identify renal evidence of obstruction, and is the preferred study for the evaluation of UJP obstruction. The radioactive tracer is usually secreted by proximal renal tubules. The half-time clearance indicates the time for half of the tracer to clear from the collecting system.  A diuretic half-time of <10 min indicates no obstruction, a half-time of 10 to 20 minutes is equivocal, and a half-time of >20 minutes suggests a high-grade obstruction. The kidney is considered significantly damaged if the split function in one kidney is less than 40% of the total kidney function. Other radiotracers can be used, such as diethylenetriamine pentaacetate (DTPA); however, these have fallen out of favor. [11] [12] [13]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Evaluation
content: Computed Tomography Urography (CTU)/Magnetic Resonance Urography (MRU) Cross-sectional imaging can provide both anatomical and functional information related to ureteropelvic junction obstruction. Urogram is a comprehensive imaging modality that can be used to diagnose multiple urologic problems in both adults and pediatrics, as it supports the provider with an accurate idea about anatomical variations, such as a crossing vessel. CTU is more commonly used in the adult population than in pediatrics due to greater exposure to ionizing radiation. In MRU, gadolinium-based contrast is used, which saves the patient from the risk of exposure to ionizing radiation

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Treatment / Management
content: A trend towards medical management with close observation has become more common. Poor drainage in pediatric patients less than 18 months old may be transient and improve spontaneously after a few months. In older patients with a split renal function of more than 40%, the renal scan should be repeated at 3, 6, and 12-month intervals. Surgery is indicated if the function has deteriorated. This is measured by creatinine levels, which may not accurately reflect renal function in newborns and infants, but no established alternative exists.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Treatment / Management
content: Conservative management in infants with severe UPJO (grade 3-4 and obstructive pattern) appears to be as effective as early surgical treatment regarding many long-term outcomes, including kidney function, growth, and hypertension. [14] Early surgery may offer more rapid improvement in anatomical severity, but the benefit over observation is not clearly superior in all measures. [14]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Treatment / Management
content: Studies suggest that about 25% of children will have mild dilatation, 50% will have moderate hydronephrosis, and 25% will have persistent severe hydronephrosis in the first 2 years of life. One retrospective study followed children diagnosed with UPJO over 16 years and found that about half could be managed conservatively, and half required surgical intervention at an average age of 10.6 months. The vast majority of patients who required surgery did so before age 4. [4] [15] Patients with urinary tract abnormalities do have higher rates of progression of kidney disease progression as adults than those without kidney disease, so they should be regularly monitored. title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Options
content: Endopyelotomy: This can be performed in either retrograde or antegrade fashion by using a cold knife or a laser to create a full-thickness incision through the lateral or posterolateral aspect of the narrowed ureteral segment. This procedure can be performed as salvage therapy for patients with disease recurrence after pyeloplasty or for those with moderate hydronephrosis or a short, strictured segment; however, it is associated with a high recurrence rate.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Treatment / Management -- Surgical Options
content: Pyeloplasty: This can be performed in patients in whom endopyelotomy is contraindicated, such as in cases of longer strictures (>1.5 cm) or crossing vessels. Open pyeloplasty Dismembered pyeloplasty (Anderson-Hynes) is the gold standard technique used by surgeons. The main advantage of this procedure is to save the crossing vessel if present. Non-dismembered pyeloplasty is used in cases of high insertion of the ureter and no crossing vessel. Laparoscopic pyeloplasty There is an ongoing debate regarding the transperitoneal versus the retroperitoneal approach There is a higher rate of conversion to open surgery with the retroperitoneal compared to the transabdominal approach. The retroperitoneal approach results in shorter operative time and hospital stay and is associated with better recovery of intestinal function. Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty may have a shorter learning curve than laparoscopic surgery, with three-dimensional visualization of instruments allowing improved mobility within the abdomen. Robotic surgery has become increasingly common in urology. New technology continues to emerge, including the adoption of single-port robotic systems. [16] [17] [18] A robotic-assisted approach to pyeloplasty is becoming increasingly widespread and is associated with shorter hospital stays, high success rates, and low complication rates. [19] One-Trocar-Assisted Pyeloplasty (OTAP) A hybrid/minimally invasive approach where parts of the surgery are done through one trocar/port, sometimes bringing the pelvis out and doing extracorporeal repair. Comparative outcomes of laparoscopic, retroperitoneoscopic, and One-Trocar-Assisted-Pyeloplasty in pediatric ureteropelvic junction obstruction demonstrated that all three procedures are effective for treating UPJO in children, with comparable success rates and low recurrence. [20] OTAP has some advantages: fewer minor postoperative complications and shorter surgery time. But it has some trade-offs: more frequent conversion to open surgery and more intraoperative minor issues. [20] Choice of technique may depend on patient age, surgeon experience, anatomical considerations, and possibly resources. Younger children may benefit more from OTAP; older ones might tolerate LP or RP better. [20]

Pyeloplasty: This can be performed in patients in whom endopyelotomy is contraindicated, such as in cases of longer strictures (>1.5 cm) or crossing vessels. Open pyeloplasty Dismembered pyeloplasty (Anderson-Hynes) is the gold standard technique used by surgeons. The main advantage of this procedure is to save the crossing vessel if present. Non-dismembered pyeloplasty is used in cases of high insertion of the ureter and no crossing vessel. Laparoscopic pyeloplasty There is an ongoing debate regarding the transperitoneal versus the retroperitoneal approach There is a higher rate of conversion to open surgery with the retroperitoneal compared to the transabdominal approach. The retroperitoneal approach results in shorter operative time and hospital stay and is associated with better recovery of intestinal function. Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty Robotic-assisted pyeloplasty may have a shorter learning curve than laparoscopic surgery, with three-dimensional visualization of instruments allowing improved mobility within the abdomen. Robotic surgery has become increasingly common in urology. New technology continues to emerge, including the adoption of single-port robotic systems. [16] [17] [18] A robotic-assisted approach to pyeloplasty is becoming increasingly widespread and is associated with shorter hospital stays, high success rates, and low complication rates. content: Medical management includes maintaining sterile urine, treating urinary tract infections, and assessing renal function and the grade of hydronephrosis on a regular basis. Rarely, a nephrectomy is indicated in cases of severe flank pain or recurrent UTIs.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Prognosis
content: Neonatal ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) and hydronephrosis gradually resolve without any surgical intervention in most of the patients. A strong correlation has been shown between the grade of hydronephrosis and the chance of spontaneous resolution. Predictors of symptomless UPJO included a postnatal anteroposterior diameter <15 mm or a stable diameter at 12 months. [22] A postnatal anteroposterior diameter cutoff of 15 mm is predictive of the need for intervention, and postnatal measurements are superior to antenatal measurements for risk stratification. [23] The Society for Fetal Urology suggested a grading system for hydronephrosis into four grades. Grade I resolves in approximately 50% of patients, and grades II, III, and IV hydronephrosis resolve in 36%, 16%, and 3% of cases, respectively. [24]

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Prognosis
content: It is important to note that children with congenital abnormalities of the kidney or ureter tract do have higher rates of progression of kidney disease as adults than children without this abnormality, so children with any such congenital abnormality should be regularly monitored.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Pregnant women are advised to attend their antenatal clinic appointments, as ureteropelvic junction obstruction (UPJO) can be diagnosed antenatally, which allows the interprofessional team to improve the management of the affected individuals. Moreover, patients with symptoms of urinary tract infections should not be neglected and should be evaluated promptly.

title: Ureteropelvic Junction Obstruction -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Providing patient-centered care for children with ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) obstruction requires a coordinated, interprofessional approach that draws upon the skills of physicians, advanced practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, and allied health professionals. Physicians and advanced practitioners must demonstrate clinical expertise in evaluating pediatric hydronephrosis, interpreting imaging studies, and determining the timing of intervention. Pediatric urologists and nephrologists play a pivotal role in selecting surgical versus non-surgical strategies, while radiologists provide critical input through accurate imaging interpretation.
